VISIT TO WINDSOR, ONT., BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
On a
question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, it is my wish to give voice to the appreciation of some fifty members of parliament and their wives who returned this morning from enjoying a magnificent trip to the great industrial city of Windsor, Ontario. This trip was arranged by the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown), and while there we were the guests of the Windsor chamber of commerce. I think it is good for members of parliament, if they are to legislate on a national basis, to take every opportunity of seeing, as widely as they can, the opportunities, industries and advantages of this country.
I cannot speak too highly of the courtesies that were extended us while we were there. Windsor calls itself the gateway to Canada's industrial progress, and I think those of us who were there are inclined to agree with that statement. That great city was a fortress for us in time of war, and we hope it will be of a source of expanding amenities in time of peace.
I find it difficult indeed to single out for specific mention any particular persons in connection with the great reception given us at Windsor, but in addition to the hon. member for Essex West, I should like to mention the other members of this parliament resident in the general area. I should like to mention the officers of the Windsor chamber of commerce. I should like to mention Mr. R. M. Sale, president of the Ford Motor Company, all his officers, and the other 14,000 men who combine to make it a great industrial team. I should like to mention Mrs. W. F. Herman, widow of the founder of the Windsor Daily Star. Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word for the Tigers and the Browns, who gave us two extra innings of superb baseball.

maintopic: VISIT TO WINDSOR, ONT., BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not rise to move any amendment, but rather to join the hon. member, and others who were privileged to be present on this referred to occasion, in expressing appreciation of the opportunity and privilege
which was ours, and of the courtesy and hospitality extended to us by the city of Windsor, the chamber of commerce of that city, the Border Cities Star, and the corporations to which the hon. member made reference. It was one of the most enjoyable and educational trips it has even been my privile^u to take.
I join with the hon. member also in thanking the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Biown), who arranged the trip, and also the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who spared no effort to make the visit a most enjoyable one.

maintopic: VISIT TO WINDSOR, ONT., BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a very happy privilege to voice the gratitude of those of us of the Social Credit party who were included in the group who journeyed to Windsor and enjoyed that most interesting tour. Indeed, we concur in all that has been said by the two previous speakers. The 'courtesies extended to this parliamentary body by the Ford Motor Company of Canada, the Windsor chamber of commerce- and we must not omit the reception of Mrs. Herman-all these courtesies we shall never forget.
We wish to extend our appreciation to the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) for their untiring efforts to make the visit so happy and so successful.
There are two things about such tours which strike me as most valuable. They bring members from all parts of Canada into closer focus with the practical business world. They broaden our views. Then, such tours are of value from another standpoint which, I think, is not too insignificant to mention here. They bring members of parliament closer together in a social friendship which is not always experienced as we sit in the House of Commons or roam the halls of this building. That, to me, in a democracy, is of inestimable value.
May I repeat, on behalf of all those associated with me in this part of the chamber, to all those who were responsible for and so thoughtful in arranging this tour: thanks a million!

maintopic: VISIT TO WINDSOR, ONT., BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Before proceeding, however, with the point of privilege I propose to raise, may I be permitted to express on behalf of the city of Windsor and the county of Essex our appreciation, of the honour conferred upon us by the visit of over fifty members of parliament and their wives.
I know I express the hope of the Ford Motor Company of Canada that other industries across the Dominion of Canada will make it possible, in as efficient a manner as it was done by the Ford Company over the past week end, for members of parliament to see the country and the people for whom we are legislating.
My point of privilege is that in the Ottawa Citizen of May 12, 1950, and repeated in the London Free Press of May 13, 1950-and I understand it also appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail on or about the same date- in making reference to the largest single exodus of members of parliament in memory on a trip to the sun parlour of Canada, it was stated that I was host to a group of automotive officials two weeks ago when they came to Ottawa to seek imposition of dumping duties on British cars.
Mr. Speaker, I was not host to any such delegation. I had no knowledge of any such delegation, and if any such delegation existed they did not communicate with me. This visit of last week end was conceived by the Windsor chamber of commerce and myself considerably over a year ago.
Further, the question I put on the order paper, and to which reference was made by the Citizen, was not at the request of the automotive industry, or any other industry or individual. It was placed thereon without the knowledge or consent of that industry.
I am interested in providing markets for our products and work for the people of Canada.
The London Free Press stated that the trip was an "expense paid affair". This statement is not correct. The members of parliament were, I believe, pleased to travel at their own 
expense to our city and to enjoy our hospitality almost as much as we enjoyed having them.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MESSAGES FROM LORD BESSBOROUGH AND OTHERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members would like me to express the appreciation we feel of the keen and constructive interest shown by His Excellency the Governor General during his visit to Winnipeg yesterday, in the truly magnificent effort being put forth both by the armed forces and the citizens themselves to combat the ravages of the Red river flood.
This morning I received a cable from a former governor general, the Earl of Bess-borough. I should like to read into our records the text of Lord Bessborough's message and of my reply, and in that way convey the message from Lord and Lady Bessborough to the people of Winnipeg and Manitoba. The cable is from Rowlands Castle, Hants, England, under date of May 13, addressed to me at Ottawa, and it reads:
Much distressed at flood disaster in Manitoba. Through you would like to express our profound sympathy for the people of Winnipeg and province in this great misfortune.
Bessborough
To this I replied:
People of Winnipeg and Manitoba will, I know, appreciate expression of distress and sympathy from yourself and Lady Bessborough, which I propose to mention in parliament today.
Then, just before coming to the house today a message was received from the Prime Minister of Italy, of which this is a translation:
Through my intermediary the government and people of Italy wish to express their sincere sympathy to the government and Canadian people, to which we are tied by bonds of friendship, on the occasion of the disaster caused by the Winnipeg flood.
I shall make answer similar to my answer to Lord Bessborough. I think these communications are a sign of the growing community of feeling that is spreading among the free peoples of the world, and one of the encouraging things which have followed upon this terrible disaster to our fellow citizens in Winnipeg and the adjoining area.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MESSAGES FROM LORD BESSBOROUGH AND OTHERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and I spent the week end in Winnipeg conferring with provincial, civic and Red Cross authorities, and with military forces, with regard to the Manitoba flood.
I thought that hon. members might like to

have a brief statement from me as to the present conditions that exist, and also as to the flood fighting activities that,are being carried on.
South of Winnipeg is a lake, in some places over twenty miles wide, and averaging twelve miles wide, extending to Emerson near the international border and for very many miles beyond that point. The Wildwood area in Fort Garry, the Kingston Crescent area, and nearly the whole of the remainder of St. Vital and the large Riverview area, are almost completely evacuated. Much of East Kildonan is largely evacuated. Most of the hospitals have been completely evacuated, and the Deer Lodge and general hospitals partly so. The city of St. Boniface is threatened on two sides, from the Red and from the Seine river, and is being protected by dikes which are in constant course of repair and which in some places are as high as twenty feet. Because of the danger which that height of dike creates, a considerable measure of evacuation of women and children from that city has been recommended and carried out.
I am glad to report that the power situation is considerably better. The power stations and gas plant have been well diked; and there is at the present time considerable optimism with regard to the ability to maintain power and light and gas services unless the river should rise substantially beyond its present level. Even should the Rover street and the Mill street substations go out, they serve only certain areas in the city and there are other substations on higher ground which could continue to serve not only their own areas by connecting power lines but other areas as well whose own substation might be put out of action.
There is no trouble expected in connection with railway access to the city.
The equipment supply has reached a peak point except with regard to pumps.
I think it will be of some relief to those who are anxious to know to be told that a well worked-out and integrated plan for complete evacuation has been prepared. The personnel of the various committees which would be required to implement this plan is already established. Zone commanders have been appointed for each evacuation zone, who would take charge immediately if the necessity arose. Emergency caches of food on both sides of the two rivers have been established to take care of the situation in the event of food warehouses being flooded. Stores of such essential materials as gasoline and motor oil sufficient to last for a considerable time in the future have been established on railway sidings in high and dry places. Emergency loading platforms have been
Manitoba Flood
established at high places for use in the event of mass evacuation, and lights have been prepared so that the evacuation may continue twenty-four hours a day if necessary.
As an indication of the thoroughness with which arrangements have been made, it is interesting to note that arrangements have been made that bread, which is a perishable product, can be brought in on a day's notice from cities outside of Winnipeg. In order to bridge that one day gap, a one day's supply of bread has been baked and frozen and is being held in cold storage. Not even that one day gap will be uncared for.
All of this is the product of what I as a Manitoban can say without immodesty is a most amazing piece of co-ordination between _ the military and civil authorities. The military authorities are acting under provincial instructions and are co-operating to the greatest possible degree with the provincial authorities, the municipal authorities, the Red Cross and the various volunteer civilian flood relief committees which have been set up.
One of the most inspiring spectacles we saw there was the Red Cross headquarters in Winnipeg, where they have three shifts of workers of between 400 and 500 each, who were operating flood lighting auxiliary services, when less than two weeks ago this service did not exist. Within that time workers in these three shifts have been brought together and placed in different branches to discharge different functions; chiefs and assistants and other ratings have been established in each branch, with the whole of this activity brought under central over-all control. All of this has been established within this short period of time; and in these three shifts there are only ten paid workers in all.
Citizens and workers of every kind, businessmen, stenographers, teletype operators, chartered accountants, lawyers, doctors in the Red Cross medical units-all these citizens are taking part in this community effort and are giving almost the entire amount of their time and effort over long hours each day to fighting this flood.
Upon the dikes themselves the work is being maintained and has been maintained from the beginning by literally thousands of volunteer workers. The figure has been given as 60,000, and while I would not want to say that it is that high, it is certainly well over 50,000. Men and women, boys and girls -some as young as twelve who work in carrying up coffee and food to the dikes-are making their contribution. I think this can best be explained in the terms of a statement made to me by a widow in East Kildonan. She told me that she was greatly relieved to be evacuated from that place because her

Manitoba Flood
young twelve year old son had been working daily from morning until late at night taking coffee and sandwiches to the workers, and he felt he had not done enough if he did not continue to carry on that effort. She could not keep him away from the dike which, as hon. members know, burst a few days ago. Luckily through good management there was no loss of life, but nearly all the pumping equipment behind the dike was lost.
All the people of Winnipeg, from the humblest schoolgirl and schoolboy to the most eminent city father, are in this fight during long days and long nights. There are numerous citizens who over a period of weeks have not averaged more than four or five hours of sleep per night. About midnight on Saturday I stood and watched as a matter of curiosity the type of traffic that was going by. There was hardly any motor traffic except trucks and cars which were loaded to capacity with dike workers, either going to or coming from their work.
I think it is proper, and I am sure that the citizens of Winnipeg and Manitoba generally would wish me to do so, to pay tribute to the fine job which the Red Cross and the armed services have been performing. Right from May 6, the day on which Premier Campbell as head of the provincial authorities instructed Brigadier General Morton to take over, he and his staff have been performing a simply magnificent feat of organization and direction. Every afternoon at 4.30 Brigadier General Morton holds a briefing session, and I was privileged to attend one of them. Each of the flood fighting heads reports briefly, succinctly, comprehensively and clearly what has happened in his area since the day before. Through the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) I should like to convey to the army the deep appreciation of the citizens of Winnipeg, of the work which the Department of National Defence has done.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: MESSAGES FROM LORD BESSBOROUGH AND OTHERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has said, I also visited Winnipeg over the week end. With me was Lieutenant General Foulkes, chief of the army general staff. Vice Admiral Grant, chief of naval services was there earlier in the week, and Air Marshal Curtis, chief of the air staff, was also in Winnipeg yesterday. Our purpose in making the visit at this time was to see what, if anything, the armed services could do in addition to what they are already doing to help to relieve the situation.
I deeply appreciate the remarks of the Minister of Justice, and also those of the premier of Manitoba, concerning the work 
of the armed forces. I shall be very glad indeed to communicate them to the services concerned.
At the present time there are actually engaged in this work in Winnipeg over 4,000 officers and men of the navy, army and air force, active and reserve. From the point of view of service participation it is a much larger operation than took place at the time of the Fraser valley floods of 1948. The services involved include some 700 of the navy, many of whom have been flown to Winnipeg from points as far distant as Esquimalt and Halifax; then there are over 2,000 army personnel, and 600 of the Royal Canadian Air Force, in addition to members of the air force engaged on the airlift. The airlift is probably the largest that has ever been carried out in Canada, with a total load already of over a million pounds, and thousands of personnel. Over thirty North Star and Dakota aircraft have been continuously engaged, with an amazing record of performance.
At the present time the aircraft are engaged in removing bed cases from the city hospitals consequent upon evacuation. By Wednesday it is expected that all Winnipeg hospitals will be evacuated, with the exception of Deer Lodge and the general hospital. These aircraft have also been carrying in large quantities of equipment of all kinds, particularly sandbags. The rate of consumption of sandbags at the present time is 300,000 a day. We have a sufficient supply available to feel that the situation is well in hand.
I should like to express to the citizens of Winnipeg the sympathy that I am sure everyone must feel for what they have gone through, and also the tremendous admiration that anyone would have who saw what we saw of the magnificent work of the civilians of Winnipeg and the adjacent communities. After all, the service personnel are doing their duty, which they are trained to do, and doing it very well indeed; but civilians are working long hours voluntarily because it is their community and their fight for their city. Leading that fight are the authorities of the provincial government, the municipalities-and there are more than ten involved-the Canadian Red Cross and dozens of agencies of various kinds, all forming a splendid working team.
I should like to conclude by reading a message I sent to Brigadier General Morton this morning on my return:
As I told the meeting of the Winnipeg flood control committee yesterday, the work being done under your direction by all personnel of the navy.

army and air force, active and reserve, working with the closest possible co-operation with civilian authorities, is a credit to the services and to our country. Our visit brought home to us the tremendous efforts that had been made and still are needed to cope with the disaster. What was most striking was the warm and friendly relationship between service and civilians at every working level. Winnipeg stands today because you stood together. Will you be good enough to convey to all ranks my appreciation and thanks for the job they are doing, and accept my hearty congratulations on your fine personal leadership. Obviously there is a long, hard fight ahead but the way you are working is the best guarantee that you will win through.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 9, consideration in committee of Bill No. 7, to incorporate Alberta Natural Gas Company -Mr. Maybank-Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

Mr. Chairman, in the discussion on this and the other private bill to incorporate a gas pipe line, the question at issue between those holding different views has remained unchanged. That question is whether or not the time has now -come, and whether or not the opportunity should be taken in connection with these bills, to insist upon writing into this legislation, or into the

legislation out of which these bills have arisen, the provision that in the construction of any such pipe lines Canada shall be served first. Those who believe that that should be done say that Canada's interests can be protected only by writing that principle into these bills. Those who take the other point of view say it is not necessary to write into the bills themselves any provision that these pipe lines shall serve this country before being built into the United States.
It is perhaps unfortunate, but certainly it is a fact, that we have been unable to reconcile those points of view. Therefore it is not my intention to dwell at any length upon the merits of one point of view or the other, because I take it that if after several weeks, to put it mildly, we have been unable to reconcile those differences of opinion, anything I may say -can hardly hope to bring about that result. I do think it important, however, to emphasize that a very significant development has taken place in the course of the discussion. The Prime Minister has now considered it appropriate, as he did on May 5, to indicate that he personally is in favour of the all-Canadian, route for these pipe lines, though he qualified his remarks to the extent of saying "if it should be found feasible to follow that route." In addition, two other hon. members who previously had either actively opposed those of us who felt that provision for the all-Canadian route should be written into the bills, or had deliberately avoided making any statement in that connection, have now clearly indicated where they stand. I refer to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano and the hon. member for Comox-Albemi.
As a member from British Columbia, a province which is most vitally concerned with these bills-though I submit I am no more concerned than any other member of this house is or should be about the principle of Canada first-I -could certainly wish that other members from my province had seen the matter as these two hon. members have seen it, and had come out in favour of the all-Canadian route, taking the position that has been taken by these two hon. members, that they will support in this house the proposition to write such a provision into these bills. There are members from the province of British Columbia who hold different views. I do not think they should be criticized. It is not the right of anyone here to criticize other members because they hold certain views. We may regret that their views are different from our own; sometimes we may become somewhat heated in our efforts to persuade them to change their views. I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that in any effort

of that sort I have made in connection with this bill or any other measure, any heat that has entered into the matter is merely a measure of my own desire to persuade those members to change their views, and is no indication that I feel they are not entitled to have views which differ from my own.
Having said that I still most earnestly ask other members from our province to reconsider their position, in the light of the fact that the Prime Minister said on May 5 that he personally favours an all-Canadian route for this pipe line, if it is feasible to build it. That is an important statement, and I suggest to those other members from British Columbia who have not yet taken a stand in favour, some of whom in fact have taken a stand against the principle which we are trying to write into this bill, that if they revise their opinion there is a good chance that we can succeed in having inserted in the bill a provision that the pipe line from Alberta to the Pacific coast shall be built first through British Columbia to Vancouver before it leaves Canada. If the other members from British Columbia would take a strong stand in favour of having that provision written into the act, enormous benefits would accrue not only to British Columbia but to the country as a whole, because it would be a victory for the principle of Canada first.
An important new aspect of this matter and of discussion of this bill is a statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce during the course of his visit to the west coast. I am not referring to the perhaps involuntary statement which he made when he referred reporters and others to an unusual source of information. I am referring to a much more deliberate statement reported in the Vancouver Sun for Wednesday, May 10, and which appears in an article bearing this headline, "Oil pipe line may follow gas to B.C." I wonder if I might be permitted to say, Mr. Chairman, that the headline of the article appears immediately below a newspaper photograph of the minister, who strangely enough, appears to be smoking.
I do not know whether it was as a result of his familiarity with that hot place to which he referred the newspaper reporters, or whether it was a matter of fulfilling his own pleasure. In any event there is the photograph, and underneath it, as I say, the headline "Oil pipe line may follow gas to B.C." The detail of the article reads in part as follows:
An oil pipe line may follow the construction of the contentious natural gas line from Alberta to the Pacific coast.
Alberta Natural Gas Company
Then a subsequent paragraph states:
In an interview in his suite in the Hotel Vancouver today,-
This paper is under date of Wednesday, May 10.
-Canada's trade minister, Hon. C. D. Howe, said there is talk in the east now of building on oil pipe line from Alberta fields to the coast.
"In fact, I have heard two or three oil companies say they are interested in this project," he added.
Like the route of a natural gas pipe line, location of a pipe carrying oil would have to be decided by the board of transport commissioners, and Mr. Howe didn't know where it would go.
Now, that is the main portion of the article referring to the statement that an oil pipe line will probably follow the construction of the gas pipe line. Immediately it comes to one's mind that we in this house have been asking repeatedly and at length for the fullest possible information in the possession of the government as to all the aspects involved in the construction of this gas pipe line. This, Mr. Chairman, is the first intimation we have had that there is any definite intention to construct an oil pipe line along the route of the gas pipe line.
Mr. Chairman, did I say anything about a proposal to construct an oil pipe line along the route of the gas pipe line? I certainly said just the opposite. I said the two projects would not be related.

I do not wish to misquote the minister. I intended to say a moment ago that this is the first intimation we have had that the construction of an oil pipe line, following the construction of the gas pipe line, is being seriously considered; that is what I intended to say, and that is what I believe I said. In any event I do not find anywhere in the article any statement from the minister that the two routes will be entirely separate. I did not intend to impute to him any statement as to the route. What I am saying is that he has informed us an oil pipe line will be constructed, following closely upon the time of the construction of a gas pipe line. If it is so, then-at any rate it was assumed by myself and by others who have taken part in this debate, and I can see no reason for assuming the opposite-that the route of the oil pipe line will follow the route of the gas pipe line, it becomes more important than ever for us to insist that the gas pipe line be built in Canada, so that the route of any pipe line serving the Pacific coast will be built through British Columbia to Vancouver first, before that line enters the United States.
In my opinion the proper place for that information to have been given as to the construction of an oil pipe line, information which appears to be peculiarly in the possession of the Minister of Trade and Commerce,

Alberta Natural Gas Company was in this house, and as soon as it came to the attention of the minister, so that it might be before the members of the house during the discussion of this most important matter.
The statement as to the possible construction of an oil pipe line and the possibility of having oil refineries in Canada, which gives a new implication to this whole question, should, if nothing else does, cause us to insist that this pipe line be located in Canada. More particularly, we should refuse to pass any bill for the incorporation of companies to construct pipe lines until either the sponsors or the government have given assurance that the lines will be built over an all-Canadian route.
While I was home recently, Mr. Chairman -and I mention this because the minister has recently been in British Columbia, and I am sure he could not fail to be impressed by the attitude of the people there toward these pipe lines-I found that the people ih both the coastal and the interior area of British Columbia were solid in their support of the principle of an all-Canadian route for this pipe line. They were unanimous, too, in their belief that such assurance should be obtained before we allow these bills to pass. Time and time again people said they could not understand why the government seems to favour the line going through the United States; why does the government not say out and out:	We will insist in this line being
built through Canada? I must confess that I cannot understand it either.
That being so, I was able to offer them no explanation of the matter except possibly this, that so far as the government is concerned it is being looked at from cold, and I submit, unrealistic so-called business points of view: How can we get the quickest return, the most dollars, for the least expenditure; if that involves sending the pipe line down through the United States, let us send it down through the United States. National policy, they say; what is that to us? Don't talk about national policy to us; we are businessmen. We want to get these natural resources down to the United States and get paid for them in the quickest possible way. This attitude on the part of the government I submit is directly contrary to the best tradition of national development, of national policy, on which this country is being built. That is the only explanation that I could offer to the people at home as to why the government seems to favour building this line straight down into the United States, instead of through Canada first.
While I was there I told my constituents that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would shortly be out in Vancouver to receive,

among other things, an honorary degree from the university, and that I felt they should let him know their views. I received word Saturday and today that no fewer than 115 separate telegrams had been sent to the minister from the Kamloops and north Thompson area while he was in Vancouver. I hope the minister got them. If he did, I am sure that those telegrams, as well as the other communications he received on the subject from British Columbia and here, have left him in no doubt about the way our people feel in this matter.
Particularly since an oil pipe line is now no longer a possibility but a probability, it becomes, as I say, doubly important to get the assurance that the route will be an allCanadian route. Therefore I want to return to what I said at the outset. I do hope that other hon. members from British Columbia will reconsider their stand. I hope that the member for Vancouver South, the member for Vancouver Centre, the member for Cariboo, and the member for Skeena-
On that score, may I say-

-'and all other hon. members from British Columbia on the government side will reconsider their attitude and see the importance of insisting that such a provision be written into this legislation. I refer particularly to the hon. member for Cariboo, because his riding is the one riding, if any riding in British Columbia stands to be benefited, which will stand to benefit most from the-
We are not supporting the Yellowhead route as the hon. member is.

-will stand to benefit most from the construction of an oil pipe line through British Columbia and Canada first. All the indications at the moment are that the main oil resources in Alberta are in the northern half of the province, in the Edmonton vicinity and north of there; and the main oil resources in British Columbia, on which exploration is now proceeding, are in the Peace river district in the northern half of the province in the hon. gentleman's constituency.
Since, as I say, it is virtually certain that the route of the oil pipe line will follow that of the gas pipe line, I submit it will be a tragedy both to the hon. gentleman's riding of Cariboo and to the province as a whole if this gas pipe line, which is now under consideration, is built down through Alberta just across the southeast corner of the province of British Columbia and then straight into the United States. It would be-
It will likely be built through Cariboo.

It would be a detriment to the future development of our province as a whole. As I say, while the hon. member is entitled to his own opinion and his own attitude, I do hope that these factors will cause him to reconsider his attitude and to join us in the fight for an all-Canadian route for this pipe line, for a route through British Columbia first to Vancouver before the line leaves Canadian soil and goes into the United States.
On the question where we should get the assurance that an all-Canadian route will be followed, there are two considerations which have emerged from the past discussion. Perhaps I might repeat briefly the general position which is taken-that is, when we are considering the request for the assurance which we have not yet received, namely, that this line will be built through Canada first.
The company whose bill is now before the committee, the Alberta Natural Gas Company, has not said it will build it on an all-Canadian route, and apparently will not commit itself to building it on an all-Canadian route. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, how we were asked in the earlier debate on second reading in this house to let the bill go to committee. We were told that that was the proper place to get the assurance. We were told: Let it go to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines; there you will be given an opportunity to call all the experts before you, to call the officials of the company and to get the assurance, if assurance there will be, *that the route will be built through Canada. What happened? It went to the committee. After three meetings, in fact during the course of the third meeting of that committee, a motion was made that no further evidence be heard; that at a subsequent meeting, the meeting immediately following that one, no further evidence be taken, and particularly no further evidence be taken as to the route of the line, but that the committee proceed to a clause by clause consideration of the bill.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
In that committee did we not hear what a great man Mr. Dixon was, the promoter?

Unfortunately I was not a
member of that committee. I have read the proceedings.

All we heard for two days was what a great man Mr. Dixon was.
Alberta Natural Gas Company
I have read the evidence fairly closely, and it may well have been that the committee was told what a great man Mr. Dixon was, although I submit-

Forty minutes of the
debate was taken up here in telling what a great man he was.

-I submit that not much concrete evidence on that particular point was submitted. Be that as it may, the committee was denied the very opportunity which the sponsor of the bill said it should have, of getting evidence on the question of the route. The motion to which I have referred, denying the committee the right to that evidence, was moved by the sponsor of the bill, who, as I read the minutes and proceedings of the committee, adopted an attitude which was completely contemptuous of the whole committee and of the question whether or not the route was a matter with which the committee should concern itself. This being so, there having been no assurance given to the committee, and the committee having been denied by the motion of the sponsor of the bill the opportunity to obtain information-there was a vote taken on the resolution which was supported unanimously by the Liberal members of the committee-we are left again in the position that the only place in which that assurance can be obtained is in this house, either, as I have said, in committee of the whole, or subsequently on third reading of the bill. And it does to my mind, at any rate, cast great doubt upon the sincerity of those who say that they too are in favour of the principle of Canada first in connection with this bill, but who so far have refrained, in their votes and in their speeches on the bill, from taking any position which would further the cause of Canada first.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, that to my mind, in view of the completely equivocal position which has now been taken on this bill, there is only one way in which any hon. member can now show whether he is in favour of Canada first or not, and that is by standing up and being counted when the vote is taken on the principle of Canada first. I think it will be found that that opportunity will be given to all members of the House of Commons. I do say again that I hope particularly those members from British Columbia on the government side of the house will bear in mind these facts in subsequent discussion.
The second feature in connection with the question of the assurance as to where the pipe line will go lies in the fact that the Prime Minister said the other day, and it has been stated frequently in the house, that the board of transport commissioners is the body to

In that connection I need only remind the committee of the magnificent speech made on Friday night by the leader of the opposition when he dealt with this question, and showed conclusively that the government does decide the route of the pipe line. He showed, by a review of the procedure in connection with the application of Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, an exactly parallel case, that before the board of transport commissioners would make their decision as to the route they required and had an assurance from an official of the Department of Trade and Commerce that that department had considered it and that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had indicated that he would give his licence for the export of oil over that particular route.
So that, as I say, in that magnificent exposition of the principle which applies in this whole question, the leader of the opposition has proven conclusively that in effect the government does have the final say as to where the route of a pipe line shall go. The leader of the opposition went on further to sum up in a manner which places on record squarely the principles this party is following, the principles of Canada first, the necessity of preserving Canada's resources for the development of Canadian industry and the development of the Canadian economy, and the necessity of following conscious policies in this and in every other connection to build up the Canadian economy on the basis of the resources we have.
There was certainly no suggestion that we should deny the export of our surplus; but it was a statement, clear and unequivocal, of the principle which we say should be followed, that before we export our raw materials in toto we must take the steps necessary to build up Canadian industry and the Canadian economy, and to preserve those resources for the ultimate, foreseeable requirements of the Canadian people.
The Prime Minister went on to say that the board could decide on the route of this pipe line, that the board was the only body which could decide on the route, and that in fact the board could refuse to grant its permission or approval if the national interest were not preserved and if the line were going to be built through the United States.
I shall read that passage of the Prime Minister's speech, because it is important


not only because of the principle he laid down but as indicating that he personally is in favour of the all-Canadian route.
This is what the Prime Minister said as reported at page 2229 of Hansard:
It has aroused public opinion-
And he was referring to the debate which had taken place in connection with these bills:
-as to the desirability of doing that if it is possible.
That is, building through Canada first.
I would expect that that would not be lost from the point of view of the members of the board of transport commissioners and that they would not lightly disregard the unanimous desire of Canadians that their own territory be used to the greatest possible advantage. I would expect that when they got an application and before they approved anything, they would want to be shown that there is or there is not a practicable way of doing it without going out of Canada.
And then at page 2230:
I suggest that unless and until we come to the conclusion that the board of transport commissioners cannot be entrusted with that kind of responsibility, because we do not feel that they are either competent enough to do it properly or sufficiently imbued with the spirit of the Canadian people to want to do it properly, the thing for us to do is to amend the Pipe Lines Act in a manner that will apply to every company that secures a charter for a pipe line and not in a manner that will discriminate in favour of one against another.
I can say with the utmost sincerity that I certainly will not question the Prime Minister's opinion as a lawyer. But I would ask him and other members of the government to consider another suggestion which I shall put forward. I have given a great deal of thought to the matter, I believe my suggestion has merit, and I would ask the government to consider it from that point of view.
The Prime Minister said that the board of transport commissioners is the only body which can decide the route, and he implied -he almost said it directly, but certainly implied and I believe meant to imply-that the board of transport commissioners could and probably should reject any application for a route, if that route did not go through Canada for a maximum total length possible before going to the United States.
I believe a reading of the Pipe Lines Act will suggest that for the board of transport commissioners to reject an application for the approval of a route solely on the ground that that route crosses the border and goes into the United States before it needs to would be an improper exercise of the authority of the board, and in fact the board in so acting would be exceeding its power, and

such action would be ultra vires of the powers of the board as laid down in the Pipe Lines Act.
A reading of the provisions of that act will disclose that a consideration of the question as to whether a pipe line crosses into the United States or not is not made a factor the board must consider when either approving or rejecting an application. The Prime Minister read the section which sets out the matters the board shall have before them when considering an application. That is not one of the matters they are empowered to consider.
However, in section 9 of the Pipe Lines Act it is clearly contemplated that a pipe line route may in fact cross the border and go into the United States. That section reads in part as follows:
A company operating a company pipe line from a place in Canada to a place on the international boundary line may exercise, beyond such boundary, in so far as permitted by the laws there in force, the powers that it may exercise in Canada.
So that by this section it is shown that the Pipe Lines Act clearly contemplates the possibility of, and thus empowers the board of transport commissioners to authorize, the construction of a pipe line from Canada into the United States. If the main Pipe Lines Act does that, and it therefore could be taken that that was done with the consent of parliament, and that parliament envisaged the construction of gas and oil pipe lines into the United States when the main act was passed, then as I have said it would be ultra vires of the board of transport commissioners to refuse to authorize any route merely on the ground that that route crosses into the United States earlier than it needs to. This would be an entirely improper exercise of their powers, because it is not made one of the factors which they shall take into consideration in approving or rejecting an application.
Following up that argument I put it forward that the board of transport commissioners has not the power to reject an application on those grounds alone. The only body with authority to say that a pipe line must be built in Canada before it crosses the boundary is, first, this parliament and, second, the government. We are asking this parliament to say that the bills now before us shall not pass until they are amended to provide that the pipe line shall be built through Canada for the maximum length before it enters the United States. If that is not done, we are content to let them pass if the government will give us assurance that they will authorize nothing but an allCanadian route.

There are two ways in which that principle can be maintained. As I have said, the first is by the government giving us assurance here and now that they will not approve any route except an all-Canadian route. That
is,	the line must be built in Canada for the maximum length to serve Canadians before it enters the United States. As the leader of the opposition pointed out last Friday, the government has that authority because it must approve the route before the board of transport commissioners in turn can approve
it.	The government must approve the route eventually, so why not now? Why not tell us now that they will require this line to follow an all-Canadian route? Why not give us that assurance following the remarks of the Prime Minister that he personally favours an all-Canadian route? Why not tell us that the government will see to it that that policy is carried out?
Following the statement made by the Prime Minister, if that simple assurance were given to this committee the debate would end immediately. I ask the government while this bill is in committee to give us that assurance. It would simply be in keeping with the personal views expressed by the Prime Minister on the 5th of May. But there is another way of arriving at the same result, an amendment to the main Pipe Lines Act to provide that any company seeking a charter must agree to build the line through Canada before the necessary permit is granted. Such an amendment would provide authority to the board of transport commissioners to reject an application on those grounds. It would expressly empower the board of transport commissioners to say, "We believe that the pipe line should follow an all-Canadian route and because you do not follow that national policy we reject your application."
Speaking for myself, and I am confident that I speak for all other members, if the government will give us assurance that they will amend the Pipe Lines Act to that effect this debate will end immediately. Here again I refer to the remarks of the Prime Minister when he indicated that that might be the proper course to follow. The Prime Minister said that the thing to do if we are not confident that the board of transport commissioners can or will do it is to amend the Pipe Lines Act which would apply to every company asking for a charter.

Mr. Chairman, I had no intention of speaking this afternoon but since my name has been brought into the discussion, perhaps I might give a report on my trip to British Columbia. I think I can supply a few facts that those who have spoken for British Columbia in this debate have perhaps omitted to give to this house.
As my hon. friend has said, I made a few statements out there. I made as few as I could. As soon as I got off the plane I was met by a reporter who demanded a statement.
I explained to him that I had made statements in the House of Commons, that the matter had been debated in the house and I did not wish to discuss it again. He got rather insistent, and I believe the leader of the opposition took the matter up in the house. It is one of my proudest possessions that I have the right to tell any man just what 1 told that reporter when he steps over the line.
However, I did a good deal of listening and I heard from a good many people. My hon. friend has referred to telegrams. Yes, I got telegrams. I got 476 telegrams.
You are not going to read them all.

I can read 350 of them in fifteen seconds, because they are identical. They read:
I endorse pipe line resolution unanimously passed by the British Columbia legislature.
That one was signed by H. Best. Another was signed by C. W. Mackenzie. Another by Tom Palmer. I have 96 more where the "I" is changed to "we". They are identical except for that. Then I have 24 where the individuals used their own wording. What happened was just as clear as could be. A man working out of Vancouver would stop at such and such a place, and I would get wires from there. He would stop at the next place, and I got 37 from there. He would stop at Kamloops and how many would my hon. friend say that I got from there?- 115.
But it was not the result of anyone coming up from Vancouver, I can assure you.

Yes, it was. If he did not visit a locality I did not receive any wires from that locality. What happened was this. Someone would arrive in a town and would open a credit with the telegraph company and then tell the people to go and send me a wire. I got a wire from Mrs. H. Best and one from Mr. H. Best. Perhaps my hon. friend can assure me that the people in Kamloops have so much money that a man and his wife would pay for identical wires just to make sure that I knew how they felt.

Those were not all from
Kamloops.

One hundred and fifteen of
them were. You could follow the man as he went along. You could almost forecast where the wires would come from next day.
I am glad the minister got them.

I was glad I got them too. The flood of wires induced me to ask one or two questions. I listened a good deal in Vancouver and I asked one or two questions. This is not a Canadian stunt. No Canadian would believe that I would be impressed by 476 duplicate wires. I may say that this filibuster is not a Canadian stunt. A filibuster running through two sessions is unique in the history of this Canadian parliament. Where does the technique come from? It comes from the United States.
Where is the pipe line going?

Mr. Chairman, I immediately demand a retraction of any statement that I have acted, or that any other member of this

house has acted, under instructions from the United States. We represent Canadian citizens, and I demand an immediate retraction.

I made no such statement. I made a suggestion as to where the technique of filibuster came from. If my hon. friend says there was no suggestion of a filibuster he could not have been- in the house. The question I asked was this. "What American pipe line company is interested in the West-coast Transmission Company?" I got the answer and I checked it. I got it from people who know and I checked it with people who know. The answer is it is the Sunray Oil Company of Delaware. Then I looked up Standard' and Poore to see how the Sunray Oil Company of Delaware is constituted. I found that Sunray is a -company which builds and operates pipe lines. The company has working capital amounting to $26 million. The Standard and Poore report shows that in 1948 Sunray made a heavy investment in Canada, including purchase of something over 20 per cent of Pacific Petroleum Company. I had always understood that Pacific Petroleum Company owned the pipe line, and I believe this company still has a substantial interest in West-coast Transmission- Company. I looked up Pacific Petroleum Company and I found that control of that -company has moved to the United States, and that within the next month the stock will be listed on- the New York curb exchange. That is interesting information. I do not think anyone has ever told this house that the battle being fought here is the battle on behalf of a United States pipe line company.
I may say that the report indicates that Sunray Oil Company is a very reliable company. They are good operators, but I did not read anywhere in the report that Sunray follows the principle of Canada first. I looked for it but it was not there. There is nothing in their charter that says they are going to build along any particular route. As a matter of fact it is not a charter; it is simply an incorporation. The matter of routes has been brought in as a red herring to cover up the effort to shut off competition for this United States pipe line company.
That is rubbish.
Statements have been made in this house-
Totally untrue and you know it better than anyone.

-that this company is going to build through the Yellowhead pass. I have asked one or two speakers what their

made an application to go through the Yellowhead pass and there has been a great deal of evidence.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of privilege, there is an innuendo there that I am acting because of representations of the Westcoast Transmission Company. That is an absolute lie, and I ask the minister to withdraw his statement.
If I have said anything unparliamentary I will be very glad to withdraw it if you will quote the statement, Mr. Chairman.
I ask for a withdrawal. No hon. member can make statements-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think the minister intended to reflect upon the hon. member.

Oh, no, it didn't.
Yes, it did. The board of transport commissioners can refuse any pipe line application. It has already refused to hear an application from Westcoast Transmission Company.
Will you refuse permits to these two companies to build through the United States?

When I have to make that decision I will have before me the proceed-

ings at a public hearing before the board of transport commissioners dealing with the route in question..
That was not the case with the Interprovincial company.

Oh, yes, it was. A public hearing was held and all the evidence was put in. After the evidence was in the Department of Trade and Commerce were asked if they were prepared to issue a permit under that act. Suppose I made a commitment to the house that a pipe line would not be built unless it went through Canada exclusively, and then it was found that it could not be so built without tunnelling through the Rocky mountains. I read in the Vancouver newspapers that a company had been incorporated in the state of Washington for the purpose of building branch lines from the pipe line coming from Canada. I do not suppose those branch lines would be built in the Yellowhead pass; I would assume they would be built somewhere down in the state of Washington, or further south. Alberta Natural Gas Company Texas. I thought it very interesting that already they are trading in Canadian gas down in the state of Washington.

He is the man who will pay for the pipe line this House of Commons is building in conversation here. He is going to pay what it costs to build the pipe line and what it costs to operate it. The man at the other end of the line is going to get what the consumer can afford to pay, less what it costs to build and operate the pipe line. If that is the situation, however, and it continues, I am afraid it will be a long time before the consumers in Vancouver get their natural gas from Alberta.
May I say a word on this? I have not taken up much time in this connection.
Oh, no?

I just moved down to the front row because my opposition moved down, and I see no reason why he should have a front seat and I should not have one as well. I do not see why we should get into a heated argument on this subject. I believe those who advocate the United States route are sincere in their belief, while those of us, particularly from the province of British Columbia, who believe in the allCanadian route are equally sincere. I give them credit for their sincerity, and I do not see why they should not give us the same credit. An hon. member from Manitoba, whose district is flooded today, keeps advising me from the rear. When my district was flooded I was home in my riding.
To bad you didn't stay there.

The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond says it is too bad I did not stay there. After his attitude toward these pipe lines I can assure him that as far as the people of British Columbia are concerned he will not be back in this house for another parliament. I just came from Windsor, where I had a very enjoyable visit.

After you walked over the Yellowhead pass route?

Alberta Natural Gas Company

Well, there is one thing about it, Mr. Chairman, the more unintelligent interruptions there are the more time will be taken up. I was hoping for a vote on this question this afternoon, and as far as I am concerned we can have that vote. While I was in Windsor I had the privilege of meeting some very prominent businessmen who belong to the chamber of commerce.
Oh, oh.
Go home and fill a sandbag. That is all you are good for.
Tell us something intelligent about the pipe line.
If I were to tell you anything intelligent you would not understand it.
We have listened to you talking in circles for a month.

I am going in squares now. As I say, while I was in Windsor I spoke to several members of the chamber of commerce. They did not know who I was, but I asked them about their gas pipe line under the Detroit river. I heard of an old widow who was seriously ill, and who had a crippled daughter. They had a gas furnace in their house, but they could not get gas; it had been shut off in Texas. All those people I spoke to, who did not know I had any connection with gas pipe lines in this house at all, told me, "Whatever you do, make very sure you have a big valve on the line where it enters the United States, so you can turn it off if you have to." Perhaps the minister did not know that gas going to Windsor was cut off in Texas. Those members of the chamber of commerce told me that certain people from the United States, and I am only taking their word for it, were in the Dominion of Canada, even in the city of Ottawa, endeavouring to make a deal by which gas would come from the Texas Panhandle through to Ontario, in return for gas through Spokane from western Alberta. I do not know whether or not that is correct, but these prominent businessmen from Windsor made that statement, and I believe it is true. I do know the name of two American businessmen from the city of New York who have been in the city of Ottawa, but I do not know whom they saw. I am here to protect the interests of my own riding to the best of my ability, and I frankly admit it; next, the interests of my own province, and then the interests of Canada.
The member for Skeena made a very reasoned speech, as he always does, and one which was well delivered. I do not agree with his arguments, but I agree with the


logical way in which he presented them. The member for Cariboo made a speech which I did not understand, and I do not think anyone else in the house did. I am sure the hon. member did not understand it himself. Then, the member for Yorkton made a speech, and all I can say about that is that he believes-that would not be parliamentary, so I shall say merely that I do not agree with him.
You are afraid of having your ears pinned back.

I am not afraid of having my ears pinned back, because as the leader of the opposition said we are trying to build a gas line to the province of British Columbia by an all-Canadian route, and not a high pressure grease route.
I want to point this out, Mr. Chairman, that not one telegram, not one letter, has come from the province of British Columbia opposing our stand in this house. If we wanted to take up the time, Mr. Chairman, we could produce articles favouring our stand. I hope the vote is taken tonight or this afternoon. As I say, there has not been a solitary letter, a solitary telegram, or a solitary organization that has endorsed the route through the United States.
If you want some telegrams, here are hundreds of them.

The minister has given me four hundred and seventy-six letters and telegrams endorsing my stand. To the best of my knowledge, there have been only three members in the house who have spoken about pipe lines who know anything about them. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a well known engineer, and he knows something about building a pipe line. The member for Coast-Capilano is, I understand, a mining engineer, and knows something about the terrain. The member for Calgary West knows the financial end of the oil business, and has acted as solicitor for various companies, as well as a speculator in the oil business of Alberta, for many years.
What do you know about it?

I know nothing about it, but I can tell you this, that I am the only member of the House of Commons who has a practical knowledge of pipe lines. I happen to be the only member of the House of Commons who owns one. It was presented to me by the most representative body in the Dominion of Canada, the parliamentary press gallery, at their annual dinner. I happen to have a pipe line of my own.

The member for Cariboo told us about Christopher Columbus, Sir Alexander Mackenzie, and the building of a route through Lillooet.
What about the associated boards of trade, and their resolution?

I happened to be at the
meeting-
It was a resolution of the associated boards of trade of the Fraser valley.
If the hon. member has not the courage to make a speech on this issue, I have. The associated boards of trade brought in a resolution favouring the allCanadian route. I happened to be at the meeting.
But by way of Prince George. The resolution came from Mission City in the hon. gentleman's own riding.

I did not understand the speech the hon. member delivered the other day, nor did anyone else. If he keeps on interrupting, I may get a little enlightenment on it. Many members have stated that the pipe line must go down through the Fraser valley. It has been stated that the Yellow-head route is the one route which has been surveyed by the most competent engineers on the North American continent, Ford, Bacon and Davis. A man from Vancouver by the name of "Jerry" Wood went over every foot of that territory. In the committee I listened with a great deal of interest to the member for Skeena tell me what a great man Mr. Dixon is. I have no doubt Mr. Dixon is a great man, and I am not disputing that fact at all. We heard all about this man, who admitted in the committee that he is a promoter.
Then there is another company, and I may as well mention that company, because I do not want to speak on pipe lines again. One representative of that company said he did not know what route the pipe line would follow; he did not know where the company was going to get the money; he did not know where they would get the gas, but he hoped they would secure a charter and hold up the other two companies. I am willing to admit that the Alberta Natural Gas Company is a legitimate company. I think it is backed by sound financial people. As for the other company, I might as. well pick up two people from amongst the funny money group, and along with myself form a company and attempt to get a charter.

You should see how funny you look.
Alberta Natural Gas Company

That may be true. While I may disagree with my minister, and while I may disagree with some of the members of my own party, some of my colleagues from my own province, no Liberal has been told he has to keep quiet, as your little group were told.
That is absolutely false.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, the member for Fraser Valley has just made a statement which I can imagine was made out of great emotion. It certainly was not made on the basis of any knowledge. If he will just carry on with his argument, I shall show him soon enough that no one has told us to keep our mouths shut. We have done so out of common decency, in the hope that someone would come to his senses and we would get this bill through.

Mr. Chairman, if my language was unparliamentary when I said they were instructed to keep quiet, I shall withdraw it. I shall put it this way: Two of their most brilliant members made excellent forty-minute speeches-
In favour of it.
-in favour of the Canadian route, and all of a sudden there was not another peep out of them. Do not tell me that no instructions were given.

Mr. Chairman, I must say once again that I am telling the hon. member there were no instructions given. I am telling him before the house that any of the members in this group can speak as he wants to speak on this subject. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, I shall assure the member for Fraser Valley, before my members, that they may vote as they desire to vote; no one is going to tell them how to vote.
I am sorry that I have been interrupted again, because it is taking up my time. I presume I shall be given a little extra time.

That is exactly what the hon.
member would do, take extra time, and that is the reason why I have kept my mouth shut up to now, because he would go right round and round; he is that kind.
